title: AI credits vs. tokens: What they mean and how to compare costs
summary: AI tokens measure model usage. Credits are a vendor-defined balance or unit. Learn why there is no fixed conversion and how to compare a credit-based plan.
body_markdown:
Tokens measure model usage. Credits are a unit or balance defined by the company selling the service. **One AI credit has no standard token value.**


To convert credits into tokens, you need the product's credit rules, the model, and the type of usage. A credit might represent money, a number of requests, or access to a feature. The label alone is not enough.


## Credits vs. tokens at a glance


Question Tokens Credits


What do they measure? Units processed or generated by a model A balance or unit the seller defines


Are they the same across products? Counts and prices can differ by model No standard definition


Do they always have one price? Input and output can have different rates A feature or model may consume different amounts


Can they expire? Tokens themselves are usage units Purchased or granted balances may expire under the terms


What should you compare? Cost for the complete task Credits consumed and money paid for the complete task


For text models, tokens can represent parts of words, whole words, or other text. Token count depends on the model and encoding; word count is only an estimate.[OpenAI's token guide](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/4936856-understanding-and-counting-tokens) explains the distinction.


## How many tokens is one AI credit?


There is no universal answer. First identify the credit model.


**Money balance:** If a credit equals a stated currency amount, divide that value by the applicable token rate. Calculate input and output separately when their rates differ.


**Fixed usage allowance:** If the plan explicitly defines a credit as a set number of tokens, use that definition and check which model and token categories it covers.


**Action credit:** If a credit buys a task, image, or request, a token conversion may not be useful. The action could include several model calls and other work.


If the seller does not publish the conversion, ask for a usage example or test the task. Do not infer the conversion from another company's plan.


## A worked conversion example


These are invented rates used only to explain the math, not the prices of any provider.


Suppose a product defines one credit as $0.01. Its example model costs $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens.


A request uses 10,000 input tokens and 2,000 output tokens:


Component Calculation Cost


Input 10,000 ÷ 1,000,000 × $2 $0.020


Output 2,000 ÷ 1,000,000 × $8 $0.016


Total $0.020 + $0.016 $0.036


That request consumes **3.6 credits** before any seller markup, other fees, or credit rounding rules.


If the output gets longer, the same input can use more credits. There is no fixed tokens-per-credit result for a changing mix of input and output.


## ChatGPT credits vs. API tokens


Start by checking which product the bill belongs to. ChatGPT and the OpenAI API have[separate billing systems](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9039756) . A ChatGPT subscription should not be treated as a general API token allowance.


For the API, a prepaid balance pays for metered usage under the account's rates and terms. It is not a promise of a fixed number of tokens across every model. OpenAI also says prepaid usage may continue briefly after the balance runs out, creating a negative balance; it is not an instant spending cutoff. See its[prepaid billing guide](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8264644-setting-up-and-managing-prepaid-api-billing) .


If a ChatGPT feature or plan offers credits, read the rules for that specific offer. Do not apply an API balance conversion to it without an explicit link in the terms.


## How to compare two AI plans


Compare the cost of a representative task, including unsuccessful attempts and retries.


1. Choose tasks you expect customers or staff to run.
2. Record the model, input, output, and any extra tool charges.
3. Record how many credits each task consumes.
4. Convert those credits into the price you actually pay for the plan.
5. Include unused or expired balances when estimating your effective cost.


For a subscription with bundled credits, dividing the subscription price by the stated allowance can give a rough unit cost. It does not prove you will use the full allowance or that all features have the same cost.


## Should an AI product charge in credits or tokens?


Use tokens when customers need a direct link to model usage and can understand the rate card. Keep model and token categories clear.


Credits can give customers one balance across several features. But the conversion must be visible enough for them to predict a bill. Show the credit cost before an expensive action and explain how price changes affect existing balances.


A credit system also needs rules for refunds, expiry, failed work, and paid versus promotional balances. Our[prepaid credit implementation guide](https://www.afternoon.co/blog/prepaid-ai-credits) covers those controls. For bookkeeping, see[how to account for AI tokens and credits](https://www.afternoon.co/blog/token-based-pricing-guide) .


## Are credits cheaper than tokens?


Neither label is inherently cheaper. Compare the same completed work, the same quality requirement, and the same usage pattern. A large allowance can still be poor value if you use little of it.
